claims.text: The component alloy is prone to hot cracking during fusion welding because of its microstructural sensitivity.
Friction stir repair uses a non-consumable rotating tool to join the damaged region.
Friction stir repair operates at temperatures below the alloy's melting point.
Replacing fusion welding with friction stir repair will restore the component's mechanical integrity.
Friction stir repair avoids melting and thereby avoids hot cracking.
Friction stir processing induces severe plastic deformation in the repair zone.
Friction stir processing induces dynamic recrystallization in the repair zone.
Dynamic recrystallization produces a refined, fine-grained repair-zone microstructure.
The refined repair-zone microstructure resists hot cracking.
Avoiding local melting prevents formation of the liquid phases responsible for hot cracking.
Mechanical stirring promotes diffusion bonding in the repaired region.
Friction-stir-induced microstructural refinement enhances mechanical resilience.
The friction stir repaired zone will have higher tensile strength than a traditional fusion-weld repair.
The friction stir repaired zone will have greater fatigue resistance than a traditional fusion-weld repair.
Friction stir repair will produce a lower incidence of hot cracking than traditional fusion-weld repair.
Traditional fusion-weld repairs create a melted and resolidified zone.
Traditional fusion-weld repairs typically exhibit hot cracking.
Traditional fusion-weld repairs have degraded mechanical performance under comparable aggressive service conditions.
Friction stir repair is applicable only where component geometry permits tool access.
The service temperature and mechanical loading must remain below limits at which the refined repair-zone microstructure becomes unstable.
